articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、AI agent & application
articles.summary: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship.

On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.

The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now.

What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.

The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live.

With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line.

But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available , and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals.

PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review.

It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.

Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository.

This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first.

Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.

Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.

Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub.

Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

articles.title: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI agent & application、Startup & business
articles.summary: Think you know where the market is headed? A startup called Supertake lets you put money behind your ideas without having to pick the stocks yourself.
articles.full_text:
AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself?

The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.

Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business.

The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV).

Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman , who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV.

He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million.

After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola.

He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April. “We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said.

While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.

The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO).

Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.

The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust.

Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.

Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time.

The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.

Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.

Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them.

For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.

For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.

Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market. “We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he says. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management.

We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.” “I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means.

The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.

Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election. “We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today.

But that being said, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.

To address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team says it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits.

For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent.

There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials. “We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” says Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing.

And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.” Access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders said they’ve put their money where their mouths are.

Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.

Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.

With the new funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others.

Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times.

The team says it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

articles.title: Google Search’s AI Mode can now tap into Drive and Wallet for more personalized responses
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、LLM engineering
articles.summary: By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that's already within its ecosystem
articles.full_text:
Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app.

Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives.

The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos.

By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem.

Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match.

Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time.

Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards.

The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money.

As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets.

By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season.

Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa.

Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context that AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses.

The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context.

AI News Tech Claude AI can review pull requests and ship fixes on its own now Anthropic is bringing new AI tools to software engineers with Claude Ship.

Anthropic is bringing new AI tools to software engineers with Claude Ship. by Jay Peters Nov 23, 2026, 8:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more.

He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code.

As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.

Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October .

What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.

PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic.

Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.

Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

articles.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
articles.summary: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully […]
articles.full_text:
AI News Policy Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’﻿ State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’﻿ by Jess Weatherbed Nov 23, 2026, 6:26 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images Part Of The latest on Grok’s gross AI deepfakes problem see all updates Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture.

Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features.

The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.” “Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses.

That was false.

Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement . “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.” Related Teens sue Elon Musk’s xAI over Grok’s AI-generated CSAM Tim Cook and Sundar Pichai are cowards X’s deepfake machine is infuriating policymakers around the globe The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos.

In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX ) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift.

In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors . xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios.

Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.

Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.

The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors: “The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards.

When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.

To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics.

We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.
